title: Pension trap punishes retirees who work
full_text:
Retiree Kim Gardner would like to return to work part-time to supplement her meagre Age Pension income but is frustrated by government rules that will penalise her for doing so.
“I would have to pay more tax and lose my pension,” said the 69-year-old Queensland woman who spent more than three decades working as a practice manager and receptionist in the healthcare sector, which is crying out for experienced staff.
“We paid a lot of tax over the years – it’s tough when you get to pension age and you still want to do something but you are fearful of doing it because you don’t want to lose your pension,” she said.
“You don’t get much pension, I can tell you. Private health insurance is over $400 a month, my insurances are $450 a month, and then there’s groceries on top, and medical bills because most of us have medical conditions… Your pension goes nowhere.” Ms Gardner is an example of a dilemma increasingly faced by older Australians, as the tax system and Age Pension eligibility rules combine to send some part-pensioners’ incomes backwards and strip more than two-thirds of the income of many others.
A report commissioned by superannuation fund Hesta has outlined the impact of Age Pension income test tapering, where a single pension reduces by 50c for every dollar earned above a $226 a fortnight threshold.
It found a pensioner with $200,000 in super earning between $15,000 and $65,000 from employment annually paid an effective marginal tax rate above 66 per cent. For a pensioner earning between $25,000 and $30,000, their effective marginal tax rate was 77 per cent, while if they earned $65,000, their effective tax rate would be 106 per cent.
The SuperEd report also found many older Australians did not even try to do extra work because they believed any paid employment would strip them entirely of their pension.
Hesta noted that the effective marginal tax rates for part-pensioners were far higher than the tax applying to younger full-time workers earning $190,000 a year.
“It’s sending a very bad message that you are penalised for working in retirement if you are on the Age Pension; we need to change that,” Hesta CEO Debby Blakey said. Hesta is calling for employment income to be removed from the income test for people on the Age Pension.
“We have about 4.5 million retirees, and we know … more than 2.5 million Australians expect to retire over the next decade,” Ms Blakey said. “Part-time work in retirement isn’t always about money or need. It can be about purpose, making a difference, staying connected to people.
“Retirement is changing and we should expect many senior Australians would want to work. Often working part-time or casually is good for their wellbeing, it’s obviously good for their bank account, and it’s also good for the economy and our community.” National Seniors Australia CEO Chris Grice said it was “unfair” pensioners were discouraged from working, and it was a missed opportunity for pensioners and the economy. Employment income could help seniors afford cost-of-living pressures, he said.
“For some, this could be the difference between keeping private health insurance or being forced into the public system. Older workforce participation would help address workforce shortages, especially important for sectors with critical shortages, such as health, aged and disability care sectors.” NSA wants employment income exempted from the Age Pension income test. Goldsborough Financial Services director Brenton Miegel said he saw many seniors juggling work and a pension. “They do it to enhance their income; often a lot do it to pay for things like holidays so they are not having to draw on super or income streams.”
